description: Confidentiality | Uses a single shared secret key to encrypt and decrypt. Fast; ideal for bulk data.
Confidentiality, Key Exchange, Signatures | Uses public/private key pairs. Slower than symmetric; used for trust and key exchange.
Confidentiality | Modern standard symmetric block cipher. AES-256 offers maximum security margin; GCM adds integrity.
Confidentiality | Secure, but AES-256 is preferred for top-secret data and post-quantum preparation.
Confidentiality | Mid-tier AES size. Most implementations standardize directly on AES-128 or AES-256.
Confidentiality | Highest standard symmetric key size. Required for top-secret classified data.
Confidentiality + Integrity | Authenticated Encryption (AEAD). The gold standard for modern TLS and bulk data protection.
Confidentiality | Legacy block cipher mode. Vulnerable to padding oracle attacks; GCM is preferred.
Confidentiality (INSECURE) | Electronic Codebook. Encrypts identical blocks identically, exposing data patterns. Never use.
Confidentiality | Turns block cipher into stream cipher using a counter. Good, but GCM is better because GCM includes integrity.
Confidentiality + Integrity | Parallelizable AEAD block mode. Standard for TLS 1.3 and IPsec.
DEPRECATED | Legacy 56-bit symmetric cipher. Broken and easily brute-forced in hours.
DEPRECATED | Applies DES three times. Slow and vulnerable to Sweet32 attack; officially retired.
DEPRECATED | Legacy stream cipher once used in WEP/SSL. Has severe keystream bias vulnerabilities.
Confidentiality | Modern stream cipher optimized for systems without hardware AES acceleration.
Confidentiality + Integrity | High-speed AEAD cipher combination. Excellent alternative to AES-GCM on mobile.
Confidentiality, Key Exchange, Signatures | Classic asymmetric cipher. Secure at 2048+ bits, but ECC is faster with smaller keys.
Confidentiality, Key Exchange, Signatures | Modern asymmetric standard. 256-bit ECC matches 3072-bit RSA security.
Integrity, Authentication, Non-repudiation | ECC-based digital signatures. Fast and lightweight.
Integrity, Authentication, Non-repudiation | Edwards-curve signature algorithm. Faster and safer against side-channel attacks than ECDSA.
Key Exchange | Classic Diffie-Hellman key exchange over insecure channels. Plain DH lacks forward secrecy unless using ephemeral keys.
Key Exchange | Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman. Fast key agreement; ephemeral version (ECDHE) provides Perfect Forward Secrecy.
Integrity | One-way transformation to fixed output. Cannot be decrypted; used for checksums and signatures.
Integrity | Secure hash family (SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512). Primary hash standard across modern security.
Integrity | 256-bit hash algorithm. Standard for digital certificates, software checksums, and TLS.
Integrity | 384-bit hash algorithm used in high-assurance and government environments.
Integrity | 512-bit hash algorithm offering maximum collision resistance in the SHA-2 family.
DEPRECATED | 128-bit legacy hash. High collision risk (two files produce same hash); completely broken.
DEPRECATED | 160-bit legacy hash. Proven collision vulnerabilities; banned in modern PKI.
Password Hashing | Modern password hash algorithm. Memory-hard to defeat GPU/ASIC cracking rigs.
Password Hashing | Blowfish-based KDF using configurable cost factors to slow down offline dictionary attacks.
Password Hashing | Memory-intensive KDF designed to stop hardware-accelerated password cracking.
Password Hashing | Key derivation function using thousands of HMAC iterations. Older standard; Argon2 is preferred.
Integrity + Authentication | Combines a secret key with a hash (e.g., HMAC-SHA256). Proves data origin and non-tampering.
Integrity, Authentication, Non-repudiation | Sign with private key, verify with public key.
CIA Triad | Ensures data cannot be read by unauthorized parties.
CIA Triad | Ensures data has not been modified or tampered with in transit or storage.
Security Goal | Verifies the claimed identity of a user, service, or packet origin.
Security Goal | Prevents a sender from denying they sent a message or signed a transaction.
Framework | Complete ecosystem of CAs, keys, and certificates managing asymmetric trust.
PKI Component | Trusted third-party authority that signs and issues X.509 certificates.
PKI Component | Electronic document signed by CA binding an identity to a public key.
Asymmetric Cryptography | Shared key used to ENCRYPT data or VERIFY a digital signature.
Asymmetric Cryptography | Secret key kept hidden. Used to DECRYPT data or CREATE a digital signature.
Protocol | Standard cryptographic protocol providing network encryption, integrity, and authentication.
Protocol | Eliminates weak ciphers, forces forward secrecy, and speeds up handshake times.
Protocol | Supported legacy TLS version. Secure only when configured with strong cipher suites.
DEPRECATED | Obsolete predecessor to TLS. SSL 2.0 and 3.0 are severely vulnerable (e.g., POODLE).
DEPRECATED | Insecure 1995 protocol. Prohibited everywhere.
DEPRECATED | Insecure 1996 protocol vulnerable to POODLE attack. Banned across all modern systems.
Protocol Suite | Network Layer (L3) VPN suite providing encryption, integrity, and authentication.
IPsec Protocol | Provides integrity and authentication ONLY. Does NOT encrypt data.
IPsec Protocol | Provides encryption (confidentiality) plus authentication and integrity.
DEPRECATED | 802.11 wireless protocol broken by 24-bit IV vulnerabilities. Cracked in minutes.
DEPRECATED | Interim wireless fix for WEP using TKIP. Obsolete.
Wi-Fi Security | Secure standard using AES with CCMP, but vulnerable to offline dictionary attacks if using PSK.
Wi-Fi Security | Modern standard using SAE to eliminate offline dictionary attacks.
WPA3 Feature | Dragonfly key exchange replacing PSK in WPA3 to defeat password guessing.
Wi-Fi Protocol | AES cipher mode used in WPA2. Replaced by GCMP in modern enterprise WPA3 setups.
Cryptographic Process | Converts plaintext to ciphertext to protect confidentiality.
Data Format | Readable original data before encryption.
Data Format | Unreadable scrambled data output produced by encryption.
Cryptographic Process | Protocol allowing parties to establish shared keys securely over open networks.
